claims.text: The magnetocaloric response of as-deposited non-equiatomic FeMnNiGeSi-type alloy films is primarily governed by local microstructural heterogeneity.
The hysteresis of these films is primarily governed by local microstructural heterogeneity.
The relevant microstructural heterogeneity consists of variations in chemical ordering and residual lattice strain.
Film deposition introduces variations in chemical ordering and residual lattice strain.
Variations in chemical ordering and residual lattice strain produce a distribution of local magnetostructural transition temperatures.
A controlled low-temperature anneal will relieve residual stress in the films.
A controlled low-temperature anneal will promote chemical homogenization in the films.
Local chemical order and residual lattice strain mediate nucleation of the magnetostructural phase change.
Local chemical order and residual lattice strain mediate the kinetics of the magnetostructural phase change.
A distribution of local transition temperatures broadens the macroscopic magnetostructural transition.
A broadened magnetostructural transition produces a moderate peak entropy change.
A broadened magnetostructural transition reduces hysteresis.
Annealing will reduce the distribution of local transition temperatures.
Annealing will consolidate the onset of the ordered hexagonal phase.
Annealed samples will exhibit a narrower transition-temperature range than as-deposited samples.
Annealed samples will exhibit a higher peak entropy change than as-deposited samples.
Annealed samples will exhibit more pronounced hysteresis than as-deposited samples during low-applied-field magnetic-cooling cycles.
As-deposited films have relatively low hysteresis compared with bulk samples having a uniform ordered state.
The proposed mechanism applies to deposited thin films in which microstructural heterogeneity and residual strain are inherent.
The annealing effect may differ in arc-melted ingots and melt-spun ribbons because their ordering and strain states differ from those of deposited films.
